stem: 50 years old man in the clinic with stressful job and high sodium diet and no physical activity bp: high (i guess it was 150/90? Im not sure) Sodium:high
OptB: ask him to monitor his bp and follow up
OptC: lifestyle changes (was more specific like less sodium and more activity)
OptD: tell him his bp is okay and nothing to worry about
highlight_terms_source: stressful job and high sodium diet and no physical activity
why_right: A 50-year-old with a high sodium diet, no physical activity and a stressful job has a mildly raised clinic BP (about 150/90, grade 1 range in ESC/WHO terms) with no organ damage, diabetes or cardiovascular disease mentioned. The first step is lifestyle modification targeted at his risk factors: salt restriction, regular aerobic exercise, weight control and stress reduction, with repeat measurements to confirm sustained hypertension before drugs are considered.
why_wrong_block:
A. Prescribed anti hypertensive immediately: right when BP is markedly high (grade 2 or more, e.g. ≥160/100), or with target organ damage, diabetes, CKD or established cardiovascular disease, or when lifestyle measures have failed.
B. Ask him to monitor his bp and follow up: confirming the reading is reasonable, but it misses the modifiable causes clearly planted in the stem; monitoring without advice is incomplete management.
D. Tell him his bp is okay and nothing to worry about: false reassurance; a BP around 150/90 is raised and needs action and follow up.
key_concept:
Mild hypertension, low risk: lifestyle first, then reassess.
  • Lifestyle: less salt, aerobic exercise, weight loss, DASH-style diet, limit alcohol, stop smoking
  • Confirm with repeated clinic, home or ambulatory readings
  • Drugs now: grade 2+ BP, organ damage, diabetes, CKD or high CV risk
  • Drugs later: lifestyle fails over a few months
  • Note: ACC/AHA calls ≥140/90 stage 2 and pairs lifestyle with a drug; ESC/NICE allow lifestyle first in low risk grade 1
exam_pearl: When the stem lists salt, inactivity and stress with mildly raised BP, the exam wants lifestyle change; drugs first only if BP is very high or there is organ damage or high risk.

stem: Pt came with cough and frothy pink sputum BP 80/40 HR 125 O2 (I think low) I think the question is asking what is true regarding the condition
why_right: Cough with frothy pink sputum means acute pulmonary edema, and with BP 80/40, HR 125 and hypoxia this is cardiogenic shock from a failing left ventricle. The body compensates for the low cardiac output with sympathetic vasoconstriction, so systemic vascular resistance rises (cold, clammy peripheries). An increased SVR is therefore the true statement.
why_wrong_block:
A. Cardiac output is decreased in cardiogenic shock (the pump has failed). A high cardiac output is the pattern of distributive shock such as sepsis (warm peripheries, low SVR).
C. Central venous pressure is normal or raised in cardiogenic shock because blood backs up behind the failing heart. A low CVP fits hypovolemic or distributive shock.
D. PCWP is raised in cardiogenic shock; that high left sided filling pressure is exactly what pushes fluid into the alveoli and causes pink frothy sputum. Low PCWP is seen in hypovolemic, septic and neurogenic shock.
key_concept:
Shock hemodynamics: identify the type, then predict CO, PCWP and SVR.
  • Cardiogenic: CO low, PCWP HIGH, SVR high
  • Hypovolemic: CO low, PCWP low, SVR high
  • Septic: CO HIGH, PCWP low, SVR low
  • Neurogenic: CO low, HR LOW (bradycardia), SVR low
  • High PCWP points to cardiogenic; high CO points to distributive (septic) shock
exam_pearl: Pink frothy sputum + hypotension = cardiogenic shock: low CO, high PCWP, high SVR.

stem: 59 have fever chills copd , dm , we give fluid bolus and bp still low
highlight_terms_source: we give fluid bolus and bp still low
why_right: Fever and chills in a 59 year old with COPD and DM who stays hypotensive after a fluid bolus is fluid refractory septic shock. Once adequate fluid has failed to restore pressure, the next step is a vasopressor to keep MAP at 65 mmHg or above, and norepinephrine is the first line vasopressor in septic shock.
why_wrong_block:
A. Dobutamine is an inotrope for low cardiac output states (cardiogenic shock, or septic shock with myocardial dysfunction despite pressors). It can vasodilate and drop BP further, so it is not the first agent for distributive hypotension.
B. Hydrocortisone is added only for refractory septic shock that persists despite adequate fluids AND ongoing vasopressor therapy. It is not given before a vasopressor.
D. More fluid is right if the initial resuscitation volume has not yet been given and the patient is still fluid responsive. Here the stem says BP is still low after fluids, which is the trigger to start a vasopressor rather than keep loading (risk of pulmonary edema).
key_concept:
Septic shock ladder:
  • Step 1: crystalloid resuscitation + cultures + early antibiotics
  • Step 2: still hypotensive after fluids → norepinephrine (target MAP ≥ 65)
  • Step 3: rising pressor needs → add vasopressin
  • Step 4: refractory shock on pressors → hydrocortisone
  • Low cardiac output despite pressors → add dobutamine
exam_pearl: No fluids yet → fluids; fluids given and BP still low → norepinephrine.

stem: A 69-year-old man complains of shortness of breath and weight loss for the last 6 months. He has a 40-pack-year smoking history and no TB or HIV risk factors (see reports). Chest X-ray: A large left-sided pleural effusion. Thoracentesis: 1,500 mL of bloody fluid that is strongly exudative by Light's criteria. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
why_right: A 69 year old, 40 pack year smoker with 6 months of weight loss and a large bloody, strongly exudative effusion has malignancy (lung cancer or mesothelioma) until proven otherwise. After the tap has been done, contrast CT chest is the next step: it shows the underlying mass, pleural thickening or nodules and lymph nodes, and maps the best target for a guided biopsy.
why_wrong_block:
A. Empirical antibiotics fit a parapneumonic effusion or empyema (fever, acute illness, purulent or low pH fluid). Six months of weight loss with a bloody effusion is not an infection picture.
C. Tissue is eventually needed, but a pleural biopsy should be image guided (CT guided or thoracoscopic) and planned after the CT; a blind biopsy before imaging has a lower yield.
key_concept:
Exudative effusion work up order:
  • Diagnostic thoracentesis: Light's criteria, cytology, culture, cell count
  • Suspected malignancy → contrast CT chest (ideally before draining the fluid fully)
  • Then tissue: CT guided or thoracoscopic pleural biopsy, or biopsy of the primary
  • Bloody effusion: malignancy, PE, trauma, TB
exam_pearl: Smoker + weight loss + bloody exudate → CT chest with contrast before any biopsy.

stem: COPD AND HAVE ACIDOSIS WHAT IS THE INITIAL INVESTIGATION
why_right: A COPD patient with acidosis (respiratory acidosis already shown on the blood gas) is having an acute exacerbation with ventilatory failure. The initial investigation is a chest X-ray to find the trigger or complication that changes management: pneumonia, pneumothorax, pulmonary edema or effusion. It is quick, bedside and done in every admitted exacerbation.
why_wrong_block:
A. Contrast CT is not an initial test in COPD exacerbation; CT pulmonary angiography is reserved for suspected PE after initial assessment, and it delays care in an acidotic patient.
C. CBC is part of routine admission bloods (white count, polycythemia, anemia) but it is supportive and does not identify the precipitant the way a chest X-ray does.
D. Sputum culture is sent when sputum is purulent or the patient is admitted, to guide antibiotics, but results are delayed and it is not the initial investigation.
key_concept:
Acute COPD exacerbation work up:
  • ABG: defines respiratory acidosis and need for NIV
  • Chest X-ray: pneumonia, pneumothorax, edema, effusion
  • ECG, CBC, electrolytes; sputum culture if purulent
  • pH < 7.35 with high PaCO2 despite treatment → NIV (BiPAP)
  • CT only for specific questions (e.g. suspected PE)
exam_pearl: Acidosis already known → next/initial investigation is the CXR to find the trigger.

stem: Case of a woman in her 30's presenting with shortness of breath and chest pain for one day. There is no cough or fever, vitally stable, labs all normal except D dimer 800 high. ECG showed peaked P wave in lead II and right deviation with right bundle branch block. What is the most helpful investigation to be done?
highlight_terms_source: shortness of breath and chest pain for one day
right deviation with right bundle branch block
why_right: Sudden "shortness of breath and chest pain" with no cough or fever, a raised D dimer, and ECG right heart strain (peaked P in II, right axis deviation, RBBB) make pulmonary embolism the working diagnosis. She is "vitally stable", so she can go to CT, and CT pulmonary angiography is the test that confirms the diagnosis.
why_wrong_block:
A. Echo shows only indirect signs (RV strain) and cannot confirm PE. It is the choice in a hemodynamically unstable patient who cannot be moved to CT.
B. A V/Q scan is used when CT contrast is contraindicated (renal impairment, contrast allergy), in pregnancy, when CTPA is inconclusive, or for chronic PE. None applies here.
D. MR angiography is not a standard first line test for PE; it is less sensitive and less available than CTPA.
key_concept:
Stable suspected PE with raised D dimer = CT pulmonary angiography.
  • D dimer: rules out PE only when negative in low probability; cannot confirm.
  • ECG: sinus tachycardia (commonest), S1Q3T3, RBBB, right axis, P pulmonale.
  • Unstable PE: bedside echo.
  • V/Q: contrast contraindicated, pregnancy, inconclusive CT, chronic PE.
exam_pearl: "Vitally stable" sends her to CTPA; hypotension would switch the answer to bedside echo.

stem: 45 k/c of HTN and 20 pack smoker, BMI 28, asymptomatic, came for check up. Best prevention for patient care? BP 150/95. Labs: HDL 1.1, LDL 4.5, Cholesterol 6.5, Triglycerides 2.1.
OptD: Lifestyle modification and follow up in 3 months
why_right: He is a "k/c of HTN" whose BP is still 150/95, and he also smokes and has LDL 4.5 mmol/L, so his cardiovascular risk is high and both factors need drug treatment. Antihypertensive therapy plus a statin is the preventive step that lowers his risk, alongside smoking cessation and lifestyle advice.
why_wrong_block:
A. Stress testing is not a screening test in an asymptomatic person; it is used to investigate exertional chest pain or other ischemic symptoms.
B. Option not recalled, so it cannot be judged.
D. Lifestyle alone with review is for newly found mild hypertension in a low risk patient without other risk factors. Here he is already hypertensive, uncontrolled, a smoker and has high LDL, so delaying drugs is inadequate.
key_concept:
Multiple risk factors + uncontrolled BP + high LDL = drug therapy for both, plus lifestyle.
  • Mild, newly found BP in a low risk patient: lifestyle first, then drugs if no response.
  • Known HTN not at target: start or step up antihypertensives.
  • Raised LDL with smoking and HTN: statin.
  • Smoking cessation is part of every answer.
  • Stress test is not for asymptomatic screening.
exam_pearl: "Known case" of HTN with BP still high is not a lifestyle only question.

stem: In a patient with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), what treatment is recommended in addition for remission and to reduce vascular complications?
highlight_terms_source: in addition for remission and to reduce vascular complications
key_concept:
SLE treatment ladder:
  • All patients: hydroxychloroquine (cornerstone)
  • Mild to moderate step 1: hydroxychloroquine + NSAID
  • Step 2: low dose steroid + hydroxychloroquine + methotrexate
  • Life-threatening: high dose steroid + immunosuppressant
  • Neuropsychiatric lupus: cyclophosphamide
  • Lupus nephritis: mycophenolate mofetil
exam_pearl: "Every lupus patient / maintain remission" points to hydroxychloroquine; "seizures or brain lesions" points to cyclophosphamide.
compiler_note:
Compiler note: Recall marks option B with '??' (uncertain); no confirmed answer.
⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: 72 yrs old mal retired free medical hx experience misbalance and i think fall" hx of osteoarthritis in his knee: he want to prevent fall and strengthen his muscle Advice him which type of exercise?
OptB: Low speed walk with swimming aerobic
highlight_terms_source: prevent fall and strengthen his muscle
key_concept:
Exercise in elderly OA and fall risk:
  • Prefer low impact: walking, swimming, water aerobics, cycling
  • Add muscle strengthening (especially quadriceps) and balance training
  • Avoid high impact: running, jumping
  • Weight loss helps knee and hip OA
  • Inactivity worsens deconditioning and fall risk
exam_pearl: In OA and fall risk the answer is almost always the low impact option; "high speed" or "running" is the trap.
compiler_note:
Compiler note: No option marked on the numbered recall. A screenshot variant (old female previously physician, afraid of falling) on the next page is carded separately with answer B.
⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: Question about old female previously physician, she want to stay active but she is afraid of falling, she suffer from osteoartheritis, whats your recommendation for her
OptB: low impact exercises like walking and aerobic water excersie
OptC: high impact exercises like jumping and running
highlight_terms_source: stay active but she is afraid of falling
why_right: She has osteoarthritis, wants to stay active, and is afraid of falling. Low impact exercise such as walking and aquatic aerobics improves strength, joint function and fitness without heavy joint loading, and water supports body weight so the fall risk during exercise is minimal. It keeps her active safely, which is exactly what she asked for.
why_wrong_block:
A. Static stretching helps flexibility as an adjunct but does not build strength, balance or aerobic fitness, so on its own it neither keeps her active nor lowers fall risk.
C. High impact exercise (jumping, running) loads the arthritic joints and increases the risk of falls and injury; it suits young people without joint disease.
D. Discouraging exercise leads to deconditioning, stiffness and weaker muscles, which worsen OA symptoms and actually increase falls; exercise is first line OA management.
key_concept:
OA exercise rule: keep moving, low impact.
  • Best: walking, swimming, water aerobics, cycling
  • Add strengthening and balance work
  • Avoid: jumping, running
  • Never: advise rest or stopping activity
exam_pearl: "Afraid of falling" points to water based, low impact exercise, not to stopping exercise.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Screenshot variant under 1407 (top of p354); Arabic line in screenshot states the correct answer is B.

stem: A patient with chronic hepatitis C presents with ascites and abdominal pain. Ascitic fluid analysis shows a neutrophil count of 300 cells/mm³. What is the most appropriate management?
why_right: Chronic hepatitis C with ascites plus abdominal pain and an ascitic neutrophil count of 300 (above the 250 cells/mm³ threshold) is spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, even without high fever. SBP needs prompt empirical systemic antibiotics, classically IV ceftriaxone (a third generation cephalosporin), before culture results.
why_wrong_block:
B. Steroids treat severe alcoholic or autoimmune hepatitis; they do not treat infection and would worsen SBP.
C. Antiviral therapy for HCV is important long term but does nothing for the acute, potentially fatal peritonitis that must be treated now.
D. TIPS is for refractory ascites or variceal bleeding; it does not treat SBP and is avoided during active infection.
key_concept:
SBP: ascitic neutrophils ≥250 cells/mm³ in a patient with ascites.
  • Clinical: abdominal pain or tenderness, fever (may be mild or absent), encephalopathy
  • Typical organism: E. coli
  • Treatment: IV ceftriaxone (third generation cephalosporin)
  • Add IV albumin when creatinine or bilirubin is raised (reduces hepatorenal syndrome)
  • Prophylaxis after an episode: ciprofloxacin
exam_pearl: Neutrophils above 250 in ascitic fluid = treat as SBP with antibiotics, regardless of temperature.

stem: Old patient diabetic, admitted to ICU with pneumonia and sepsis. What is the most appropriate empiric therapy in addition to azithromycin?
why_right: This is severe community acquired pneumonia (ICU, sepsis) in an elderly diabetic, and the lead-in says "in addition to azithromycin". The standard regimen for admitted or ICU CAP is a beta-lactam such as ceftriaxone (covers pneumococcus and common gram-negatives) plus a macrolide (covers atypicals), so ceftriaxone completes the pair.
why_wrong_block:
A. Moxifloxacin is an alternative to the beta-lactam plus macrolide combination, not an add-on to azithromycin; adding it duplicates atypical coverage and adds QT risk. It is the choice when a single comorbid-CAP agent is asked for.
B. Vancomycin covers MRSA only and is added when there are MRSA risk factors (prior MRSA, recent IV antibiotics, post influenza necrotizing pneumonia); none is given here.
key_concept:
Empirical CAP therapy:
  • Healthy outpatient: macrolide (azithromycin)
  • Comorbid: respiratory fluoroquinolone (levofloxacin, moxifloxacin) OR beta-lactam + macrolide
  • Admitted or ICU: ceftriaxone + azithromycin (or beta-lactam + fluoroquinolone)
  • MRSA risk: add vancomycin or linezolid
  • Pseudomonas risk or HAP: antipseudomonal beta-lactam (piperacillin/tazobactam, meropenem)
exam_pearl: Read the lead-in: "in addition to azithromycin" asks for the beta-lactam (ceftriaxone); a variant without that phrase asking for a single comorbid-CAP drug is keyed to moxifloxacin.

stem: Old in 50s or 60s KC of HTN and DM, signs of dehydration. Came complaining of severe vomiting and diarrhea. A week ago she had an appointment with her primary physician Cr was 60, now her creatinine is 160. The cause of kidney injury? Urine sodium 60, urine osmolality 220, specific gravity 900, BUN 11.
why_right: This recall's key is pre-renal azotemia because the story is volume loss: severe vomiting and diarrhea, signs of dehydration, and creatinine rising from 60 to 160 within a week in a previously stable patient. Hypovolemia reduces renal perfusion, and pre-renal AKI from dehydration is reversible with IV fluids; the recaller summarized the case as dehydration.
why_wrong_block:
B. Acute on chronic kidney injury needs evidence of pre-existing CKD; her baseline creatinine one week ago was normal (60), so there is no chronic disease to build on.
C. ATN is the intrinsic injury that follows prolonged or severe hypoperfusion (or nephrotoxins, contrast) and shows high urine sodium (above 40), low urine osmolality (below 300) and a FeNa above 2%; the recaller's summary pointed to simple dehydration.
key_concept:
Pre-renal vs intrinsic (ATN) AKI indices:
  • Urine sodium: pre-renal <20; ATN >40
  • FeNa: pre-renal <1%; ATN >2%
  • Urine osmolality: pre-renal >500 (concentrated); ATN <300
  • Specific gravity: pre-renal >1.010; ATN about 1.010 or less
  • BUN:creatinine: pre-renal >20:1
  • Diuretics can raise urine sodium even in pre-renal AKI
exam_pearl: History of fluid loss suggests pre-renal, but if urine sodium is high and urine is dilute, the injury has progressed to ATN.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Recaller notes the case was long with many labs; summary is that she was dehydrated; sure of the three options. Typed recall lists 'A. Pre renal azotemia' as the answer.

stem: A 28-year-old man who recently joined military service and underwent excessive military training presents to the Emergency Department with lightheadedness on standing and fatigue. Physical examination reveals postural hypotension, otherwise unremarkable. Urine osmolality is elevated >500 mOsm/kg. What is the most likely etiology for his acute kidney injury?
why_right: Excessive military training causes volume loss, and postural hypotension confirms hypovolemia. A urine osmolality > 500 means the tubules are intact and concentrating urine maximally, which defines pre-renal azotemia.
why_wrong_block:
B. AIN is intrinsic renal injury; damaged tubules cannot concentrate, so urine osmolality is low (< 300), and it usually follows a drug.
C. Glomerulonephritis is intrinsic renal disease with hematuria, RBC casts, edema and hypertension rather than postural hypotension.
D. ATN can follow prolonged hypovolemia, but tubular damage gives dilute urine (< 300) and FeNa > 2%; a concentrated urine means the tubules still work.
key_concept:
Pre-renal vs intrinsic AKI indices:
  • Urine osmolality: > 500 pre-renal; < 300 intrinsic
  • FeNa: < 1% pre-renal; > 2% ATN
  • Urine Na: low pre-renal; high ATN
  • BUN:Cr: > 20 pre-renal
  • Sediment: bland pre-renal; muddy brown casts ATN
exam_pearl: Concentrated urine (> 500) = tubules working = pre-renal; if exertion also gave dark urine and high CK, think rhabdomyolysis.
compiler_note:
Repeats: appears 3× in this file (also AS-0004, AS-2501).
Compiler note: Unnumbered related question placed under 1417.

stem: A 16-year-old man presented to the Outpatient Department complaining of diarrhea for 3 years. He was passing 3-4 large volumes of stool per day, which was foul smelling and contained undigested food but no blood or mucus. He was also complaining of postprandial bloating and easy fatigability. On examination, he looked pale and has no secondary sexual characteristics, BMI 14 kg/m2. Hb 10 (130-170 g/L), MCV 70 (80-95), platelets 433 (150-400 x 10^9/L), ALT 90 (5-40 IU/L), AST 60 (12-40 IU/L), ESR 12 (2-10 mm/h). Which of the following is the most appropriate diagnostic test?
why_right: A 16-year-old with 3 years of large, foul smelling stools with undigested food (malabsorption), bloating, BMI 14, no secondary sexual characteristics (delayed puberty), microcytic anemia (iron malabsorption) and mildly raised transaminases is a classic picture of celiac disease. The appropriate diagnostic test among the options is celiac serology, IgA anti-endomysial antibodies, followed by duodenal biopsy for confirmation.
why_wrong_block:
A. Fecal fat confirms steatorrhea but cannot tell which malabsorptive disease is responsible, so it does not make the diagnosis.
B. Barium follow through is nonspecific imaging used mainly for small bowel Crohn disease (strictures, fistulae); there is no blood or mucus and the ESR is only trivially raised, so Crohn is not suggested and it cannot diagnose celiac disease.
C. The lactose breath test diagnoses lactose intolerance, which causes bloating and diarrhea but not growth failure, delayed puberty or iron deficiency anemia.
key_concept:
Celiac disease workup:
  • Clues: chronic diarrhea, bloating, weight loss, low BMI, iron deficiency anemia, raised transaminases, short stature or delayed puberty
  • Associations: type 1 diabetes, dermatitis herpetiformis
  • Initial serology: IgA tTG (with total IgA); EMA is the alternative serology
  • Confirm: duodenal biopsy (villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, intraepithelial lymphocytes)
  • Treatment: gluten free diet; follow compliance with tTG
exam_pearl: If tTG is not among the options, anti-endomysial antibody is the celiac serology to choose.

stem: A 40-year-old man presented to the emergency department with fever, severe headache, neck stiffness, and photophobia for two days. On physical examination, the physician asked the patient to flex his neck forward. This maneuver caused involuntary flexion of the patient hips and knees. Which of the following clinical signs is demonstrated in this patient?
highlight_terms_source: involuntary flexion of the patient hips and knees
why_right: In a patient with meningitis features (fever, headache, neck stiffness, photophobia), passive flexion of the neck that produces involuntary flexion of the hips and knees is the Brudzinski (neck) sign. It reflects meningeal irritation: stretching the inflamed meninges triggers reflex flexion of the lower limbs.
why_wrong_block:
A. Kernig sign is elicited with the hip flexed to 90 degrees: extending the knee is resisted or painful. It tests the legs, not neck flexion.
B. Babinski sign is an upgoing big toe on stroking the sole, indicating an upper motor neuron lesion; it is not a meningeal sign.
D. Romberg sign is loss of balance on standing with feet together and eyes closed, indicating sensory (proprioceptive) ataxia from dorsal column or peripheral nerve disease.
key_concept:
Bedside signs:
  • Brudzinski: neck flexion causes hip and knee flexion (meningism)
  • Kernig: hip flexed 90, knee extension painful or resisted (meningism)
  • Babinski: upgoing plantar (UMN lesion)
  • Romberg: falls with eyes closed (sensory ataxia)
  • Meningeal signs have low sensitivity; a negative sign does not exclude meningitis
exam_pearl: Brudzinski = Bend the neck (legs flex); Kernig = Knee extension (hip flexed).

stem: How long should H. pylori triple therapy be used:
why_right: H. pylori eradication regimens (PPI plus two antibiotics, classically amoxicillin and clarithromycin) are short antibiotic courses given for 7 to 14 days. The question asks for the duration of triple therapy, which is a course measured in days, not weeks or months.
why_wrong_block:
B. Three months is far longer than any eradication course; prolonged antibiotics add side effects and resistance without benefit. Long courses belong to things like TB therapy, not H. pylori.
C. Four weeks is the interval to wait after finishing antibiotics before retesting for eradication (urea breath test), not the treatment duration. A PPI may be continued longer to heal an ulcer, but the triple therapy itself is not 4 weeks.
key_concept:
H. pylori: treat with a short antibiotic course, then confirm eradication.
  • First line: PPI + amoxicillin + clarithromycin for 7 to 14 days
  • Failure: quadruple therapy (PPI + bismuth + metronidazole + tetracycline)
  • Test of cure: urea breath test, at least 4 weeks after antibiotics
  • Stop PPI about 2 weeks before the breath test to avoid false negatives
exam_pearl: Do not confuse the 4 week wait before retesting with the 7 to 14 day treatment course; current practice favours the full 14 days.

stem: Persistent HTN , FH OF STROKE , potassium 3,2 , muscle proximal 4/5 what test to reach diagnosis ?
key_concept:
Hypertension + low K: decide between aldosterone excess and cortisol excess by the body habitus.
  • No Cushingoid features: aldosterone:renin ratio (Conn)
  • Obesity, striae, diabetes, bruising: 24 h urine free cortisol, late night salivary cortisol or 1 mg dexamethasone test
  • Both can cause hypokalemia and proximal weakness
  • Familial early stroke + hyperaldosteronism: glucocorticoid remediable aldosteronism
exam_pearl: Proximal weakness alone does not mean Cushing: hypokalemia itself causes muscle weakness, so look for the Cushingoid body features.
compiler_note:
Compiler note: Options written inline in the recall (Urine cortisol 24 h / Aldosterone renin ratio); no answer marked.
⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: A patient develops arthritis after Clostridioides difficile infection. What is the most likely explanation?
why_right: Arthritis that follows a GI (or GU) infection, with sterile joint cultures, is reactive arthritis. The clue is the sequence "arthritis after C. difficile infection": the joint is inflamed by an immune reaction to a distant infection, not infected itself. It is typically asymmetric, may migrate between joints and can come with enthesitis (e.g. Achilles), conjunctivitis or urethritis.
why_wrong_block: B. Septic arthritis is direct joint infection: usually one hot joint with positive synovial fluid culture and a high neutrophil count. It would be right if the aspirate grew organisms; a preceding diarrhoeal illness alone points to a reactive process.
key_concept:
Arthritis 1 to 4 weeks after a GI or GU infection with sterile cultures = reactive arthritis.
  • Triggers: enteric organisms (including C. difficile) or Chlamydia
  • Features: asymmetric, migratory oligoarthritis, enthesitis, conjunctivitis, urethritis
  • Other options to consider: gonococcal arthritis (sexual exposure, tenosynovitis, pustules), IBD arthritis (chronic bloody diarrhoea)
  • Treatment ladder: NSAID, then sulfasalazine if severe; treat any ongoing infection
exam_pearl: Positive joint culture flips the answer to septic arthritis; sterile joint after a recent diarrhoea or urethritis = reactive.

stem: Elderly women known DM HTN has a history of IHD years before. Came complaining of increasing shortness of breath, increased when she lay down. No chest pain, no other complains. Vitals normal. (The question came with 2 clear pictures) First picture ECG showing ST-elevation in leads II, I, AvF, V5 and V6 only. The second picture chest x-ray showed pulmonary edema. What is the cause of this patient complaint?
highlight_terms_source: shortness of breath, increased when she lay down
ECG showing ST-elevation in leads II, I, AvF, V5 and V6
why_right: The patient's complaint is shortness of breath worse on lying down (orthopnoea), and the chest X-ray shows pulmonary edema; fluid in the alveoli is what directly produces this breathlessness. The question asks for the cause of the complaint, and the source keys the radiological finding that explains it, with no chest pain and normal vitals.
why_wrong_block:
A. Acute coronary syndrome would be favoured by chest pain or dynamic ECG change with raised troponin; here there is no chest pain and a remote IHD history, so the ST elevation (I, II, aVF, V5 to V6) is taken as background change rather than the reason for the breathlessness in this key.
C. Pulmonary embolism gives sudden dyspnoea with pleuritic pain, tachycardia, hypoxia and often a clear chest X-ray; it does not cause orthopnoea or radiological pulmonary edema.
D. Decompensated heart failure is the underlying syndrome that can produce pulmonary edema, but the key names the finding that directly explains the orthopnoea; it would be the answer if the stem asked for the underlying diagnosis.
key_concept:
Orthopnoea + alveolar edema on chest X-ray = pulmonary edema as the cause of dyspnoea.
  • ST elevation territories: II, III, aVF inferior; I, aVL, V5 to V6 lateral; V1 to V4 anterior
  • Old MI with persistent ST elevation can reflect a ventricular aneurysm
  • Diabetic elderly women may have ischaemia without chest pain (dyspnoea as anginal equivalent)
  • PE: sudden dyspnoea, clear lungs, tachycardia, risk factors
exam_pearl: The lead-in is 'cause of the complaint', so the key is the finding that produces the symptom, not the background disease.

stem: A 45-year-old man was admitted to the ICU with fever. He required a vasopressor to maintain a MAP of more than 65 mm Hg. He is receiving adequate IV fluid resuscitation. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: The decisive clue is that he "required a vasopressor to maintain MAP > 65 mm Hg" despite "adequate IV fluid resuscitation". Hypotension that persists after fluids and needs vasopressors, in a febrile (infected) patient, defines septic shock, the most severe stage of the sepsis continuum.
why_wrong_block:
A. Sepsis is infection with a dysregulated host response (older model: SIRS plus infection); it does not by itself imply vasopressor dependent hypotension. It would be right if he were infected and unwell but normotensive.
B. Septicemia is an outdated, non defined term for bacteria in the blood with systemic illness; it is not a stage of the sepsis continuum.
D. SIRS is only 2 or more inflammatory criteria (temperature, HR, RR, WBC) without a required infection or hypotension; it fits a post operative inflammatory picture with normal BP.
key_concept:
Sepsis continuum: pick the highest stage the stem proves.
  • SIRS: 2 or more of temp, HR, RR/PaCO2, WBC criteria
  • Sepsis: SIRS (or organ dysfunction) + suspected/confirmed infection
  • Severe sepsis (older term): sepsis + organ dysfunction
  • Septic shock: hypotension needing vasopressors for MAP ≥ 65 despite adequate fluids
  • Sepsis-3 also requires lactate > 2 mmol/L for septic shock
exam_pearl: "Vasopressor despite adequate fluids" is the phrase that upgrades sepsis to septic shock.
compiler_note:
Terse recall of the same question: Patient has pneumonia and need excessive fluid and norepinephrine to maintain normal BP is it sepsis, SIRS, septicemia, septic shock?
Compiler note: Screenshot of similar recall (0084) with Answer: C.

stem: Celiac case with dermatitis herpetiformis. A 29-year-old man diagnosed with celiac disease 2 years ago. He complains of ongoing diarrhoea, feeling tired and bloating. Poor compliance with a gluten-free diet is suspected. Which of the following is the most appropriate method to ascertain this?
highlight_terms_source: Poor compliance with a gluten-free diet is suspected
why_right: In a known celiac with ongoing symptoms and "poor compliance with a gluten-free diet suspected", the objective test of adherence is IgA tissue transglutaminase (tTG). On a strict gluten-free diet the tTG level should fall over about a year; a persistently high level means continued gluten exposure. It is quantitative, cheap and non-invasive, so it is the monitoring test of choice.
why_wrong_block:
A. A food diary is subjective and misses hidden or accidental gluten; useful for dietitian counselling, but it cannot objectively confirm exposure.
B. Duodenal biopsy is invasive; it is used to confirm the initial diagnosis or to assess persistent symptoms despite proven adherence (suspected refractory celiac), not as the first check of compliance.
C. Anti-endomysial antibodies are a second-line, confirmatory serology; tTG IgA is the preferred, quantitative test for both screening and follow-up.
key_concept:
tTG IgA screens for celiac disease and monitors gluten-free diet adherence.
  • Diagnosis: tTG IgA, then duodenal biopsy (villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, intraepithelial lymphocytes)
  • EMA: second-line confirmatory serology
  • Test while still eating gluten, or results are falsely negative
  • Compliant patient: tTG falls over about a year
  • Symptoms despite negative tTG and good adherence: think refractory celiac, re-biopsy
exam_pearl: Suspected non-compliance = tTG level; persistent symptoms despite proven compliance = biopsy.

stem: A 25-year-old patient presented with diarrhea for 5 months, which is mostly related to eating bread and wheat products. Which of the following skin lesions would suggest the likely diagnosis?
why_right: Chronic diarrhoea "related to eating bread and wheat products" points to celiac disease, and its classic skin marker is dermatitis herpetiformis: intensely itchy grouped papules and vesicles on extensor surfaces (elbows, knees, buttocks). It reflects the same gluten sensitivity and improves with a gluten-free diet (dapsone for the itch).
why_wrong_block:
A. Psoriasis gives well-demarcated silvery plaques and is linked with psoriatic arthritis; it is not the skin marker of gluten enteropathy.
B. Hyperpigmentation points to Addison disease, haemochromatosis or Whipple disease; it would be the answer if the stem described hypotension, weakness or skin creases darkening.
D. Pyoderma gangrenosum is an extraintestinal sign of inflammatory bowel disease (especially ulcerative colitis); choose it when diarrhoea is bloody and chronic, not gluten-triggered.
key_concept:
Gluten-triggered diarrhoea + itchy extensor vesicles = celiac disease with dermatitis herpetiformis.
  • Celiac associations: type 1 DM, dermatitis herpetiformis, iron deficiency
  • IBD skin: pyoderma gangrenosum, erythema nodosum
  • Addison: hyperpigmentation of creases and gums
  • DH treatment: gluten-free diet, dapsone for symptoms
exam_pearl: Pyoderma gangrenosum and erythema nodosum point to IBD; the celiac skin sign is dermatitis herpetiformis.

stem: A 35-year-old man is evaluated during a follow-up visit. He is a known case of rheumatoid arthritis that is well controlled with prednisone 15 mg and hydroxychloroquine 400 mg daily. His physical examinations are unremarkable (see lab results). Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
why_right: He is "well controlled" but on prednisone 15 mg daily with hydroxychloroquine as his only DMARD. Steroids in RA are a bridge and must be tapered because of long term toxicity, and needing 15 mg prednisone to stay controlled shows hydroxychloroquine alone is not adequate disease control. Methotrexate is the anchor DMARD, so the plan is to taper prednisone and start methotrexate.
why_wrong_block:
B. Ibuprofen is an NSAID that only relieves symptoms and does not modify disease; it cannot replace a DMARD and suits mild disease only.
C. Cyclosporine is a second line agent in RA because of nephrotoxicity and hypertension; it is not used in place of methotrexate, the anchor DMARD.
D. Continuing would leave him on long term moderate dose steroid with hydroxychloroquine monotherapy; good control on steroids is not a reason to stay on them.
key_concept:
RA: steroids bridge, DMARDs maintain, methotrexate is the anchor.
  • New active RA: methotrexate (± hydroxychloroquine) + short steroid bridge
  • On steroids long term: taper and secure a DMARD
  • Active despite methotrexate: add a biologic (e.g. TNF inhibitor such as adalimumab)
  • NSAIDs: symptom relief only
  • Cyclosporine and azathioprine: not preferred in RA
exam_pearl: "Well controlled" on prednisone is a trap: the answer is still to taper the steroid and start methotrexate.

stem: A 30-year-old woman with stable systemic lupus erythematosus presents to the clinic with active polyarthritis for 1 week. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
why_right: A patient with stable SLE whose only active problem is polyarthritis has mild to moderate (joint) lupus with no organ threat. Hydroxychloroquine is the background drug for every lupus patient; when arthritis is active despite it, the next step is a low-dose steroid plus methotrexate, the preferred steroid-sparing DMARD for lupus joints and skin.
why_wrong_block:
B. Sulfasalazine is a rheumatoid/spondyloarthritis DMARD, not a preferred agent in SLE, and it can provoke lupus flares or drug reactions.
C. Cyclophosphamide is reserved for severe organ-threatening lupus, classically neuropsychiatric lupus (and severe nephritis); it is far too toxic for isolated arthritis.
D. Mycophenolate mofetil is first line for lupus nephritis (proteinuria, raised creatinine); there is no renal involvement here.
key_concept:
Match the SLE add-on to the organ involved.
  • All patients: hydroxychloroquine (cornerstone)
  • Joints/skin, mild to moderate: low-dose steroid + methotrexate
  • Kidney (nephritis): high-dose steroid + MMF
  • CNS (neuropsychiatric): high-dose steroid + cyclophosphamide
  • Planning pregnancy: switch MMF/MTX to azathioprine, keep HCQ
exam_pearl: Arthritis only = methotrexate; nephritis = MMF; CNS lupus = cyclophosphamide. Sulfasalazine is the RA distractor.

stem: 20 year old woman with no previous medical illnesses presented with a 7 day history of increasing jaundice, nausea, vomiting and right sided upper abdominal pain (see lab results). Which of the following tests has the greatest prognostic value? Total bilirubin 26 (3.5-16.5 umol/l); AST 700 (12-40 IU/L); ALT 1650 (5-40 IU/L); ALP 126 (39-127 IU/l).
why_right: A young woman with 7 days of jaundice and ALT 1650 has acute hepatitis; the lead-in asks for the greatest prognostic value. Prothrombin time (INR) reflects synthesis of short half-life clotting factors, so it is the earliest and best marker of hepatic function and of progression to acute liver failure.
why_wrong_block:
A. Bilirubin reflects excretion and cholestasis; it is a weaker short-term prognostic marker than PT in acute hepatitis.
B. Albumin has a long half-life (about 3 weeks), so it does not fall early in acute injury; it reflects chronic synthetic function, as in cirrhosis.
D. ALT measures hepatocyte injury, not function, and does not predict outcome; a rapidly falling ALT can even mean massive necrosis with few hepatocytes left.
key_concept:
Transaminases show injury; PT/INR shows function and prognosis.
  • Acute hepatitis prognosis: PT/INR (plus encephalopathy)
  • Chronic synthetic function: albumin
  • Falling ALT with rising INR and bilirubin = ominous
  • ALT > AST: viral, drug or autoimmune hepatitis
exam_pearl: 'Prognostic' in acute liver injury = PT/INR; very high ALT is not a prognostic marker.

stem: Which of the following diagnostic tools is the best option for screening for hepatocellular carcinoma in cirrhotic patients?
why_right: HCC screening in cirrhosis is abdominal ultrasound every 6 months, with or without AFP. When only one tool is chosen, ultrasound takes priority because it is safe, cheap and detects focal lesions directly.
why_wrong_block:
A. Liver function tests assess hepatic injury and synthesis; they do not detect a tumour and are not a screening test for HCC.
B. AFP is an adjunct with limited sensitivity and specificity; many HCCs do not raise it, so it is not the best single screening tool.
D. Triphasic CT is for characterising a lesion over 1 cm found on screening ultrasound, not for routine surveillance (cost, contrast and radiation).
key_concept:
Cirrhosis: ultrasound (± AFP) every 6 months for HCC surveillance.
  • Nodule < 1 cm: repeat ultrasound in about 3 months
  • Nodule > 1 cm: triphasic CT or contrast MRI
  • Typical arterial enhancement and washout = HCC, no biopsy needed
  • Cured HCV with cirrhosis still needs surveillance
exam_pearl: Screening = ultrasound; characterising a found lesion = triphasic CT or MRI.

stem: 62-year-old woman with a long standing history of pruritus and fatigue presented with a 2-months history of jaundice and abdominal swelling. Scratch marks seen. Jaundiced with clubbing. Splenomegaly with ascites. Labs: RBC 4, Hb 11, Platelets 102, WBC 3, INR 1.5, ALP 170, ALT 78, AST 112. US Abdomen: coarse liver with 3 cm focal lesion at rt lobe. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
OptD: Triphasic CT scan of the abdomen
highlight_terms_source: coarse liver with 3 cm focal lesion
why_right: This woman is cirrhotic ("coarse liver", splenomegaly, ascites, low platelets, INR 1.5), likely on a cholestatic background (long pruritus, raised ALP). A 3 cm focal lesion on ultrasound is a positive HCC screen, and any nodule over 1 cm needs a multiphasic contrast study: triphasic CT (or contrast MRI). Typical arterial enhancement with washout diagnoses HCC without biopsy.
why_wrong_block:
A. AFP is an adjunct that neither confirms nor excludes HCC; a nodule over 1 cm still needs contrast imaging whatever the AFP.
B. Biopsy is reserved for when contrast CT/MRI is non-diagnostic; it carries bleeding and tract-seeding risk, especially with coagulopathy and ascites as here.
C. Doppler assesses vessel patency (portal or hepatic vein thrombosis) but cannot show the enhancement pattern needed to characterise the lesion.
key_concept:
Liver nodule in cirrhosis: size decides the next step.
  • < 1 cm: repeat ultrasound in about 3 months
  • > 1 cm: triphasic (multiphasic) CT or contrast MRI
  • Typical pattern (arterial enhancement + washout): HCC, no biopsy
  • Non-diagnostic: the other contrast study or biopsy
exam_pearl: Biopsy is not the next step for a cirrhotic liver nodule; contrast imaging comes first.

stem: A patient with meningitis has cerebrospinal fluid findings of SLIGHTLY low glucose and high lymphocytes and high Protein. What is the most appropriate treatment? They literally wrote 'SLIGHTLY low glucose', no encephalitis symptoms, just meningitis
key_concept:
Read cell type and glucose together.
  • Neutrophils + low glucose: bacterial → ceftriaxone + vancomycin + dexamethasone
  • Lymphocytes + normal glucose: viral → supportive, acyclovir if HSV suspected
  • Lymphocytes + low glucose + subacute course: TB → anti-TB therapy + steroid
  • If the LP result is given, treat by the result, not empirically
exam_pearl: Any glucose reduction makes pure viral meningitis less likely; think partially treated bacterial or TB.
compiler_note: ⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: IV drug user presents with S&S of meningitis. CSF analysis show: glucose = 250 (Normal 250-500) Blood glucose <0.4 lymphocytic predominance. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
OptD: Fungal meningitis (Aseptic Meningitis In Other Recalls)
why_right: The CSF shows lymphocytic predominance with a CSF to blood glucose ratio < 0.4 (low glucose). Lymphocytes plus low glucose is the TB meningitis pattern, and an IV drug user is at higher risk of TB (and HIV). Bacterial meningitis would be neutrophilic; viral would have normal glucose.
why_wrong_block:
A. Viral meningitis is lymphocytic but keeps glucose normal (ratio above about 0.6); the low ratio here rules it out.
C. Bacterial meningitis lowers glucose but with neutrophil predominance and an acute course; choose it if the CSF were PMN-rich.
D. Cryptococcal meningitis can also give lymphocytes with low glucose and is a real consideration because IV drug use carries an HIV risk; choose it with known advanced HIV, very high opening pressure or a positive cryptococcal antigen/India ink. The 'aseptic meningitis' wording of this option means a viral-type CSF with normal glucose, which the ratio < 0.4 excludes.
key_concept:
CSF cell type + glucose ratio decide the organism.
  • Neutrophils + ratio < 0.4: bacterial
  • Lymphocytes + ratio > 0.6: viral
  • Lymphocytes + ratio < 0.4: TB
  • TB clues: subacute weeks-long course, endemic origin, high protein, cranial nerve palsies
exam_pearl: Lymphocytes alone do not mean viral; add low glucose and the answer becomes TB.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Screenshot of the same <0.4 version (printed below 1466) also gives B. Tuberculous meningitis. CSF summary: PMN + ratio <0.4 bacterial; lymphocyte + ratio >0.6 viral; lymphocyte + ratio <0.4 TB; cryptococcal: lymphocyte + ratio >0.6; non-cryptococcal fungi: PMN + ratio <0.4.

stem: IV drug user presents with S&S of meningitis. CSF analysis show: glucose = 250 (Normal 250-500) Blood glucose >0.4 lymphocytic predominance. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: The CSF shows lymphocytic predominance with a CSF:blood glucose ratio above 0.4, so glucose is not consumed: this excludes the low-glucose meningitides (bacterial, TB). A lymphocytic, normal-glucose, culture-negative picture is the definition of aseptic meningitis, the umbrella term the recall keys here. In an IV drug user the aseptic group includes viruses (HIV seroconversion, enteroviruses, HSV) as well as non-infective and partially treated causes, which is why the broader label is chosen.
why_wrong_block:
A. Viral meningitis gives exactly this CSF (lymphocytes, normal glucose) and is the commonest cause of aseptic meningitis; the recall keys the broader category instead. Pick viral when aseptic is not offered.
B. TB meningitis is lymphocytic but with low CSF glucose (ratio below 0.4) and high protein, usually after weeks of fever; the ratio here is not low.
C. Bacterial meningitis is neutrophil predominant with low glucose (ratio below 0.4) and turbid CSF; neither feature is present.
key_concept:
Read CSF by cell type first, then CSF:serum glucose ratio.
  • Neutrophils + low ratio: bacterial
  • Lymphocytes + normal ratio: viral / aseptic
  • Lymphocytes + low ratio + high protein: TB
  • Cryptococcal: lymphocytes; other fungi can be neutrophilic with low glucose
  • Aseptic = culture-negative meningitis; viral is its commonest cause
exam_pearl: Lymphocytes alone do not mean viral: a LOW glucose ratio with lymphocytes means TB.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Summary of CSF analysis: PMN + CSF:serum glucose ratio <0.4 bacterial; lymphocyte + ratio >0.6 viral; lymphocyte + ratio <0.4 TB; fungi: cryptococcal lymphocyte + ratio >0.6, non-cryptococcal PMN + ratio <0.4.

stem: Pt has meningitis, lymphocytes predominance and glu 2.5 (lower normal) w low serum glu, dx?
why_right: Lymphocytic predominance narrows it to viral or TB. CSF glucose of 2.5 looks borderline, but the stem says the serum glucose is also low, so the CSF:serum ratio stays normal; there is no true glucose consumption. Lymphocytes with a normal glucose ratio is the classic viral meningitis picture.
why_wrong_block:
A. Bacterial meningitis is neutrophil predominant with a truly low glucose ratio (below 0.4); this CSF is lymphocytic.
C. Aseptic meningitis is the umbrella for culture-negative meningitis with this same CSF; when a specific cause (viral) is offered, choose the specific, commonest one.
D. TB meningitis is lymphocytic but with a low ratio, high protein and a subacute course over weeks; here the low CSF value is explained by the low serum glucose.
key_concept:
Always interpret CSF glucose against serum glucose.
  • Normal ratio is about 0.6; below 0.4 means consumption
  • Low serum glucose lowers CSF glucose without meningeal disease
  • Neutrophils + low ratio: bacterial
  • Lymphocytes + normal ratio: viral
  • Lymphocytes + low ratio + high protein: TB
exam_pearl: A 'low' CSF glucose is meaningless until you check the blood glucose; hypoglycaemia mimics TB or bacterial CSF.

stem: A patient presents with signs & symptoms of meningitis. Lumbar puncture: CSF glucose: 5 mmol/L, CSF protein: 700 mg/L (reference range: 100-400 mg/L), Predominant lymphocytes. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for the specific causative organism?
why_right: The CSF shows predominant lymphocytes, normal glucose (3.5 mmol/L) and only mildly raised protein (500 mg/L), which is a viral pattern. When the LP result is given, treat according to it: the treatable viral cause to cover is herpes simplex, so IV acyclovir is the specific therapy.
why_wrong_block:
A. Ceftriaxone and vancomycin: the bacterial meningitis regimen, right with neutrophil predominant CSF, low glucose and high protein; not a lymphocytic CSF with normal glucose.
B. IV methylprednisolone: steroids (dexamethasone) are an adjunct in bacterial meningitis, and high dose methylprednisolone is for relapses of demyelinating disease; neither treats a viral organism.
C. Antifungal therapy: right for cryptococcal meningitis, typically in immunocompromised (HIV) patients with lymphocytes and LOW glucose; no such clue here.
key_concept:
If the CSF result is given, treat the organism it points to, not the empirical cocktail.
  • Neutrophils + low glucose: ceftriaxone + vancomycin + dexamethasone
  • Lymphocytes + normal glucose: viral, IV acyclovir (HSV)
  • Lymphocytes + low glucose: TB (or fungal if immunocompromised)
  • Unknown CSF, sick patient: empirical ceftriaxone + vancomycin + dexamethasone + acyclovir
exam_pearl: Confusion, seizures or temporal lobe changes with a lymphocytic CSF = HSV encephalitis; acyclovir should never be delayed.

stem: A woman with hypertension is found to have a renal bruit on physical examination. What is the most appropriate next investigation?
why_right: Hypertension with a renal bruit points to renal artery stenosis, a classic, correctable secondary cause of hypertension. The lead-in asks for the next investigation, so the non-invasive, radiation-free first test is chosen: renal ultrasound with Doppler, which shows asymmetric kidney size (small affected kidney) and stenotic flow.
why_wrong_block:
A. CT angiography is the confirmatory, more definitive test once ultrasound suggests stenosis (answer it when the lead-in says 'confirm' or 'best'), but it needs iodinated contrast and is not the first step.
C. MR angiography is an alternative confirmatory test, used when iodinated contrast must be avoided; it is not the initial screen.
D. Plain X-ray cannot show the renal arteries or kidney perfusion and has no role in renovascular hypertension.
key_concept:
Renal artery stenosis: screen non-invasively, then confirm.
  • Clues: renal bruit, resistant or new severe HTN, rise in creatinine after ACE inhibitor/ARB, asymmetric kidneys
  • Initial / next: renal Doppler ultrasound
  • Confirmatory: CT or MR angiography
  • Gold standard: catheter renal angiography
exam_pearl: Lead-in verb decides it: 'next / initial' = Doppler US; 'confirm / most accurate' = angiography.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Initial, next -> US best. Most appropriate, confirmatory -> CT.

stem: 60-year-old man with a history of osteoarthritis of the left knee presents with chest pain on exertion relieved by rest. Resting ECG and cardiac enzymes are normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in evaluation?
highlight_terms_source: chest pain on exertion relieved by rest
why_right: Chest pain on exertion relieved by rest is typical stable angina, and with a normal resting ECG and enzymes the next step is a stress test. The decisive clue is osteoarthritis of the knee: he cannot exercise adequately, so a pharmacologic stress test is used, here dobutamine stress echocardiography.
why_wrong_block:
A. Exercise ECG is the choice when the resting ECG is normal AND the patient can exercise; knee osteoarthritis prevents reaching target heart rate.
B. Resting echocardiography assesses structure and function but does not provoke ischaemia, so it cannot diagnose stable angina.
C. CT coronary angiography is an anatomical test; in this exam algorithm a functional stress test comes first, and angiography follows a positive stress test.
key_concept:
Stable chest pain workup: resting ECG decides the stress test.
  • Normal ECG + can exercise: exercise ECG
  • Normal ECG + cannot exercise: dobutamine stress echo or pharmacologic nuclear scan
  • Abnormal resting ECG (LBBB, LVH, paced, digoxin): stress echo or nuclear imaging
  • Positive stress test: coronary angiography
exam_pearl: Any reason he cannot walk (OA, amputation, claudication) turns exercise ECG into pharmacologic stress.

stem: If patient comes with celiac disease with symptoms of diarrhea weight loss (more sx) also has arthritis or joint pain, not on medications, in his 20's 30's; they did a test and + Tissue transglutaminase, also RF was a bit high. What is the most appropriate management?
why_right: Diarrhoea, weight loss and a positive tissue transglutaminase antibody establish celiac disease, and its treatment is a lifelong gluten-free diet. The joint pain is an extra-intestinal manifestation of celiac disease that usually settles on the diet, and a slightly raised RF is non-specific, so it does not justify RA treatment in a patient who is not on any medication.
why_wrong_block:
B. Steroids are reserved for refractory celiac disease that fails a strict gluten-free diet; they are not first line.
C. Methotrexate treats established rheumatoid arthritis; a mildly raised RF with celiac arthralgia does not make an RA diagnosis.
key_concept:
Celiac disease: diagnose with tTG IgA, treat with gluten-free diet.
  • Screen: tTG IgA (check total IgA)
  • Confirm: duodenal biopsy (villous atrophy) while still eating gluten
  • Treat: lifelong strict gluten-free diet
  • Monitor adherence: repeat tTG
  • Refractory disease only: steroids or immunosuppression
  • Extra-intestinal: iron deficiency, arthralgia, dermatitis herpetiformis, osteoporosis
exam_pearl: A mildly raised RF is a distractor; joint pain in celiac disease is treated by the diet, not DMARDs.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Embedded screenshot: child with weight loss, joint pain (knees), anemia, positive anti-transglutaminase IgA and elevated rheumatoid factor; A- Gluten-free diet, B- Corticosteroids. Answer: A.

stem: A 35-year-old woman presented to the clinic with a 3-month history of fatigue, lethargy, and weight gain. Physical examination is unremarkable (see lab results). Which of the following is the most appropriate investigation?
why_right: "Fatigue, lethargy and weight gain" over 3 months with a normal exam raises suspicion of hypothyroidism. TSH is the single best first test for thyroid dysfunction because it is the most sensitive marker of primary thyroid disease; further tests depend on its result.
why_wrong_block:
B. TPO antibodies identify the cause (Hashimoto thyroiditis) once dysfunction is confirmed, or guide management of subclinical hypothyroidism; they are not the first test.
C. T3 is not used to assess hypothyroidism and is measured, if at all, after TSH (mainly in suspected T3 toxicosis).
D. Free T4 is checked after an abnormal TSH (or together with it if pituitary disease is suspected); alone it is not the initial screen.
key_concept:
Thyroid work up ladder: TSH first.
  • Step 1: TSH
  • Step 2: free T4 (± T3) if TSH abnormal
  • Step 3: TPO antibodies for the cause (Hashimoto)
  • High TSH + low fT4 = overt primary hypothyroidism
  • High TSH + normal fT4 = subclinical hypothyroidism
exam_pearl: TPO is tempting because Hashimoto is common in young women, but you confirm dysfunction (TSH) before looking for its cause.
compiler_note: Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-0399B).

stem: A 50-year-old man referred to the clinic with positive HCV. He is asymptomatic with no history of drug use or previous blood transfusion. Physical examination was unremarkable. Lab tests showed normal LFT with positive anti-HCV (ELISA), HCV RNA was negative. US abdomen showed normal liver. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
why_right: Positive anti-HCV with negative HCV RNA means either resolved past infection or a false positive antibody, not active hepatitis C. He is asymptomatic with no risk exposure, normal LFTs and a normal liver on ultrasound, so he needs reassurance and no further testing.
why_wrong_block:
A. Liver fibroscan: used to stage fibrosis in confirmed chronic HCV (positive RNA) before treatment; there is no active infection here to stage.
C. Triphasic CT scan of liver: used to characterize a liver mass or suspected HCC, typically in cirrhosis; his liver is normal on ultrasound.
D. Repeat HCV RNA in 6 months: appropriate if there was a recent exposure (window period) or ongoing risk; this man has no exposure history and normal enzymes.
key_concept:
HCV antibody tells you exposure; HCV RNA tells you current infection.
  • Ab+ / RNA+ → active infection: assess fibrosis, genotype, treat with DAAs
  • Ab+ / RNA− → cleared infection or false positive
  • Ab+ / RNA− with no exposure and normal enzymes → reassure, no further tests
  • Ab+ / RNA− with recent exposure → repeat RNA later
exam_pearl: A recent exposure (needle stick, new IV drug use) turns Ab+/RNA− from reassurance into repeat RNA testing.
compiler_note: Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-1573).

stem: Patient is evaluated for overload picture (crackles, LL pitting edema). Denied any history of trauma. OE: raised JVP, distant heart sound, hypotensive 90/70. Xr: wide cardiac silhouette. ECG: high voltage. Which area of heart is affected?
why_right: Raised JVP, distant heart sounds and hypotension are Beck's triad, and a wide cardiac silhouette with no trauma points to a large pericardial effusion with tamponade physiology. The process sits in the pericardium. The original question describes a low voltage ECG (fluid damping the signal); 'high voltage' in this recall is very likely a memory slip.
why_wrong_block:
A. Myocardial disease (cardiomyopathy, myocarditis) causes failure and arrhythmias; a truly high-voltage ECG would suggest LVH, but muffled sounds with Beck's triad point to pericardial fluid.
C. Coronary artery disease presents with ischaemic chest pain and ST/T changes, not muffled sounds with a globular heart.
D. Endocardial disease (endocarditis, valve lesions) gives murmurs, fever and embolic signs, not distant heart sounds and tamponade.
key_concept:
Cardiac tamponade = pericardial effusion compressing the heart.
  • Beck's triad: hypotension, raised JVP, muffled heart sounds
  • Pulsus paradoxus
  • ECG: low voltage, electrical alternans
  • CXR: enlarged globular (water-bottle) heart
  • Diagnosis: echocardiography; unstable: pericardiocentesis
exam_pearl: Distant sounds + big heart + LOW voltage = effusion; HIGH voltage would mean LVH.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Screenshot 0145: 42M, SOB, fever, high JVP, pulsus paradoxus, distant heart sounds, ECG low voltage, CXR increased cardiac silhouette; Answer: B Pericardium. Comment: muffled heart sounds = effusion (B), high voltage = LVH (A); recaller likely wrote 'high' by mistake; if truly high voltage, no answer fits.

stem: 34-year-old man, known case of ulcerative colitis on azathioprine and tapering steroid, presented with 6-7 bloody bowel motions, lower abdominal pain and low grade fever. Stool culture negative. Stool for Clostridium difficile toxins positive. BP 110/70, HR 100, T 38.4 °C, SpO2 95%. Hb 11, Plt 456, WBC 16, ESR 67, Albumin 29. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
highlight_terms_source: Stool for Clostridium difficile toxins positive
why_right: The decisive clue is a positive C. difficile toxin in an immunosuppressed UC patient (azathioprine plus steroids), so this flare is C. difficile infection. First-line treatment is oral vancomycin (or fidaxomicin); it must be given orally because it acts in the colonic lumen. WBC 16 (above 15) and albumin 29 (below 30) mark a severe episode, where metronidazole is not adequate.
why_wrong_block:
A. Tinidazole is for Giardia and amoebiasis; it is not a C. difficile treatment.
B. Cephalosporins do not treat C. difficile and are a classic cause of it.
D. Metronidazole is no longer first line; IV metronidazole is only added to oral vancomycin in fulminant disease (shock, ileus, megacolon).
key_concept:
C. difficile: always test in IBD flares; treat with oral agents.
  • First line: oral vancomycin or oral fidaxomicin
  • IV vancomycin does not reach the colon
  • Fulminant (shock, ileus, megacolon): oral/rectal vancomycin + IV metronidazole, surgical review
  • Stop the offending antibiotic if possible
exam_pearl: Vancomycin for C. difficile is ORAL; IV vancomycin is the trap.

stem: A patient with A-fib on warfarin for stroke prevention presented with nosebleed and bruises, recently took herbal supplements. His INR is 4. What to do?
OptC: Advice to stop herbal and recheck INR
why_right: The INR of 4 is only modestly above the AF target of 2 to 3, the bleeding is minor (nosebleed and bruises), and there is a clear reversible cause: recent herbal supplements interacting with warfarin. The recall's key is to remove the interacting product and recheck the INR, keeping the patient on anticoagulation for stroke prevention rather than abandoning it.
why_wrong_block:
A. Stopping warfarin altogether removes stroke protection in AF; a supratherapeutic INR is managed by withholding doses and correcting the cause, not by discontinuation.
B. Aspirin does not adequately prevent stroke in AF and still carries bleeding risk; it is not a substitute for anticoagulation.
key_concept:
High INR on warfarin: first ask 'is there bleeding?', then the INR level.
  • No bleeding, INR 4 to 10: hold warfarin, close follow up, consider low-dose oral vitamin K
  • No bleeding, INR above 10: hold warfarin + oral vitamin K
  • Major bleeding: admit, IV vitamin K + PCC or FFP
  • Always look for the cause: interacting drugs, herbs, diet, illness
exam_pearl: Find the cause of a rising INR (herbs, antibiotics, diet); stopping anticoagulation in AF is rarely the answer.

stem: A 60-year-old man with a 6-month history of exertional shortness of breath. Positive Corrigan pulse, early diastolic murmur at the left upper sternal border, bilateral fine basal crepitations. Echo: Severe aortic regurgitation and ejection fraction of 40%. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
why_right: The Corrigan's pulse plus an early diastolic murmur at the left upper sternal border is aortic regurgitation, and echo confirms it is severe. He is symptomatic (6 months of exertional dyspnea, basal crepitations) and the LV is already failing (EF 40%). Symptomatic severe AR, or severe AR with LV systolic dysfunction, is a surgical lesion: aortic valve replacement is the only option that corrects the cause.
why_wrong_block:
A. Diuretics only relieve the pulmonary congestion; they do not fix the leaking valve and do not stop LV deterioration. Right as a short-term symptomatic bridge, never as definitive therapy here.
B. Vasodilators such as dihydropyridine CCBs reduce afterload in AR but are for patients who cannot or will not have surgery (or for hypertension); they do not replace AVR in symptomatic severe AR.
D. ACE inhibitors are supportive for the reduced EF or for nonsurgical candidates; they do not delay the need for valve surgery once symptoms or LV dysfunction appear.
key_concept:
Severe AR: when to operate (AVR)
  • Symptoms (dyspnea, angina, HF) = AVR
  • Asymptomatic but LV dysfunction (reduced EF) = AVR
  • Asymptomatic, normal LV = follow-up with serial echo
  • Vasodilators (CCB, ACEi) = only if surgery not possible or for BP
  • Signs: Corrigan (water-hammer) pulse, wide pulse pressure, early diastolic decrescendo murmur, louder sitting forward
exam_pearl: Any valve lesion that is severe AND symptomatic goes to surgery; medical therapy is the answer only for the asymptomatic or inoperable patient.

stem: A 68-year-old man with COPD presents with worsening shortness of breath, productive cough, and confusion. Using accessory muscles, RR 32/min, SpO2 85% on room air. ABG pH 7.28, PaCO2 65, PaO2 55. Which finding indicates that this COPD exacerbation is severe and requires urgent intervention?
why_right: The lead-in asks which finding marks a severe, life-threatening exacerbation. Confusion / decreased level of consciousness reflects CO2 narcosis from hypercapnic respiratory failure (PaCO2 65, pH 7.28) and signals the need for urgent ventilatory support, and for intubation rather than NIV if consciousness is significantly impaired.
why_wrong_block:
A. Productive cough is a feature of almost every infective exacerbation and says nothing about severity.
B. SpO2 92% sits in the COPD target range of 88 to 92%; it is reassuring, not a severity marker (the patient's actual SpO2 is 85%).
D. Mild wheezing implies air is moving; a silent chest, not mild wheeze, would be ominous.
key_concept:
Severe / life-threatening COPD exacerbation markers.
  • Confusion, drowsiness, decreased consciousness
  • Respiratory acidosis: pH below 7.35 with raised PaCO2
  • Accessory muscle use, high RR, inability to speak
  • Cyanosis, hypoxaemia despite oxygen, haemodynamic instability
  • Alert + acidosis despite treatment: NIV; impaired consciousness or failing NIV: intubation
exam_pearl: In COPD, SpO2 88 to 92% is the target, not a danger sign; confusion is the red flag.

stem: Young patient with high BP, also his 2 sisters and his parents also hypertensive. No proteinuria. What treatment to start?
why_right: A young patient whose parents and sisters are all hypertensive has primary (essential) hypertension with a strong familial pattern, not a secondary cause. For a patient under 55, step 1 drug therapy is an ACE inhibitor (or ARB). The phrase "no proteinuria" does not change this: the ACE inhibitor is first line by age, and proteinuria would only add a renoprotective reason.
why_wrong_block:
A. A thiazide-like diuretic is added at step 2 with an ACE inhibitor or CCB; it is not the first pick for a young patient in this pathway (also an option when a CCB is unsuitable in older patients).
B. Beta blockers are not first line for uncomplicated hypertension; they are chosen for a compelling indication (post-MI, angina, HFrEF, AF rate control) or late in resistant hypertension.
D. Alpha blockers are reserved for resistant hypertension (step 4, especially when K+ is high) or pheochromocytoma pre-operatively, not initial therapy.
key_concept:
First-line antihypertensive depends on age and origin.
  • Under 55 or diabetic: ACE inhibitor or ARB
  • Over 55 or African/Caribbean origin: CCB
  • Step 2: ACEi/ARB + CCB or thiazide-like diuretic
  • Step 3: ACEi/ARB + CCB + thiazide-like diuretic
  • Step 4 (resistant): spironolactone if K+ low, else alpha or beta blocker
exam_pearl: Young + strong family history = essential hypertension, so treat by age (ACEi); a young hypertensive WITHOUT family history or with clues (hypokalemia, renal bruit, paroxysms) needs a secondary cause workup first.

stem: Patient with jerky movement in one arm (myoclonic seizure) given valproic acid and failed, what to give?
why_right: Jerky movements of a limb are myoclonic seizures, a generalized seizure type. When valproic acid failed, the next choice is another broad-spectrum antiepileptic, and levetiracetam is the preferred one for myoclonic seizures (effective, few interactions, well tolerated).
why_wrong_block:
B. Phenytoin is a narrow-spectrum sodium channel blocker that can AGGRAVATE myoclonic and absence seizures; it is used for focal seizures and as second line in status epilepticus.
C. Phenobarbital is broad but sedating with cognitive and behavioural effects, so it is kept for later lines or status epilepticus, not as the next oral agent after valproate.
key_concept:
Match the antiepileptic to the seizure type.
  • Generalized/myoclonic: valproate first, levetiracetam next (valproate avoided in women of childbearing potential)
  • Absence: ethosuximide (child), valproate if also GTC
  • Focal: carbamazepine or lamotrigine
  • Drugs that worsen myoclonus/absence: phenytoin, carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, gabapentin
exam_pearl: Myoclonic seizures + sodium channel blocker (phenytoin, carbamazepine) is the classic trap: they make myoclonus worse.
